6. Example: Analysis of Competing Hypotheses in Action

Do not write one favoured hypothesis in detail and make the alternatives caricatures. Ask people with different knowledge to generate possibilities. Include a normal explanation, a technical explanation, an intentional explanation only when warranted, and an “other” or combined case when the space is genuinely open.
Worked example: a sudden fall in three-site attendance

Use five alternatives: H1 port disruption; H2 factory quality hold; H3 demand spike consuming available inventory; H4 administrative data error; H5 combined port and factory effects. The combined case prevents false either-or reasoning, but it should not become a refuge that absorbs every contradiction. Define what additional pattern a combined explanation predicts.

Analysts independently rate a training case, discuss disagreements and revise the handbook—not merely their scores. Preserve examples of borderline calls. Calibration improves shared language without forcing identical judgment.

Ask a reviewer to construct the strongest case for the second-ranked hypothesis and the strongest reason the leading hypothesis could be wrong. The reviewer may identify an omitted mechanism, dependent evidence or a collection blind spot. Red teaming should challenge the logic, not reward contrarian performance.

Record prediction, issue time, probability or verbal confidence, resolution rule and outcome. Do not edit a prediction after the event. Review calibration across many cases rather than celebrating one correct call. A method that produces clear reasoning but systematically overconfident forecasts still needs repair.

Analysis of Competing Hypotheses, often abbreviated as ACH, is a structured analytic technique for evaluating several plausible explanations for the same set of facts. Instead of asking, “What evidence supports my preferred view?” ACH asks, “Which hypothesis is least inconsistent with the evidence we have?” That shift is the heart of the method.

It is a decision-making and intelligence framework used when signals are ambiguous, evidence is incomplete, and smart people can reasonably disagree about what is happening. Consultants frequently use it in
ACH was developed and popularized by Richards J. Heuer Jr., a longtime CIA analyst. Heuer has written that he developed the method in the late 1970s, and he later explained it in detail in

The method was created to address a familiar problem: analysts tend to settle too quickly on an initial narrative and then collect evidence that supports it. In intelligence, that can lead to serious errors. In business, the same failure mode shows up when leadership teams misread a competitor’s intent, interpret a market signal too narrowly, or confuse a plausible story with the most likely one.

The method is especially powerful when there are three to five genuinely plausible explanations and the available evidence is mixed. It is also useful when the team is politically invested in a particular answer, because the framework forces disagreement into the open. Used well, ACH often becomes an entry point into broader
